# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
## The report's claim

At 24 months, Varden's case-processing offices still show a per-hour gain over control:

| Hours measure | Gain at 24 months |
|---|---|
| Timesheets | +9.8% (down from +12.5% at 9 months) |
| System logs | +8.5% |

Output per employee is −3.4%. A registered mediation analysis attributes about half the per-hour gain to fewer meetings and about a fifth to reduced fatigue. The county ended the counter arm at month 12 because waiting times rose. Among Halden organisations with records, continuers show about +11.8% per actual hour, and the three that reverted had coverage or deadline pressures.

This is the strongest document so far. It takes on the open questions from the earlier documents, uses the tests that were missing, and is mostly hedged appropriately in the body. The problems are mainly in the Summary and in a few places where its own data complicate its interpretation.

I checked the arithmetic:

| Check | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% |
| Per-hour gain, logs | 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% |
| Halden continuers, hours | 34.9 / 40.3 | −13.4% |
| Halden continuers, per-hour gain | 96.8 / 86.6 | +11.8% |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100 |

## 1. The control group was contaminated, and that bears on the "decay"

At month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their own standing meetings, and their output per hour then rose 4.1%. That raises the control comparison and shrinks the treated-versus-control difference. Roughly, two of seven offices at +4.1% for the last nine months could account for a point or more of the drop from 12.5% to 9.8%.

The report presents the meeting audit only as evidence about mechanism. It should also estimate the 24-month effect excluding those two offices, or with an adjustment, before attributing the decline to fading. The audit itself may be a spillover from treated offices in the same county, which is interesting in its own right.

There's also an arithmetic puzzle here. If two control offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours of meetings, the control mean should drop by about 0.6 hours, not from 7.2 to 7.0. Either the other five control offices increased their meetings or the averages need checking.

## 2. What do system logs measure, given that meetings were cut?

Logs record "time staff are working on cases." If that excludes meetings, the numbers are hard to reconcile. Treated staff cut meetings by about 3.5 hours a week, so case-work time should have fallen far less than total hours:

- Baseline: about 37.9 total hours minus 7.4 hours of meetings leaves about 30.5 hours of case work.
- Month 24: about 33.4 total hours minus 3.9 hours of meetings leaves about 29.5 hours of case work.
- That is a fall of about 3%, not the reported 11%.

If logs instead include meetings (staff logged in while in a meeting), they aren't a stricter measure of work. The report needs to define the log measure, because it is both the headline denominator and the outcome in the mediation model.

## 3. The mediation result is promising but not "confirmed"

- **The same offices generated and tested the hypothesis.** Registering at month 11 guards against choosing the analysis after seeing the data. But it doesn't make the result an independent replication, since the seven treated offices that suggested the hypothesis also tested it. "Larger sample of office-months" adds time, not independent units; the effective sample is still 14 offices.
- **Measurement error favours meetings over fatigue.** Meetings come from calendar data, which is objective and precise. Fatigue is self-reported, which is noisier. Noise in a mediator biases its estimated share downward, so the 47%-versus-18% split partly reflects how each was measured.
- **The mediators weren't randomised.** Offices whose managers cut meetings most may differ in other ways, such as management quality. The Limitations note this; the Summary's "confirms" doesn't.

The body's word, "survives," is about right. The Summary should use it too.

## 4. The Summary mixes measures and absorbs a counterexample

- **Two measures in one comparison.** "Fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months" compares timesheets with logs. The like-for-like decline is 12.5% to 9.8%, about a fifth. The body handles this correctly; the Summary doesn't. (§5's "about a quarter" is also between the two.)
- **The reversions don't all fit the coverage story.** "All with client-facing or coverage obligations" folds in a marketing agency that reverted over client deadlines. Halden classed marketing as office work, and the meta-analysis would code it as discretionary. Deadline pressure in discretionary work is a different failure mode from coverage, and it deserves to be stated as one rather than merged into the coverage story.

## 5. Outcomes still missing

- **Backlog and time to decision** in case-processing offices were not reported at nine months and still aren't. With output per employee at −3.4% (CI down to −8.0%) for two years, the queue may have grown. This is the clearest way the public could be worse off without it showing up in cases closed, and the 9-month Limitations named it as the risk to watch.
- **Cost per case.** Pay is unchanged, output per employee is −3.4%, and staff may be paid overtime, so cost per case has probably risen by several percent. Lower turnover (4.1% vs 7.9%) may offset part of that. The county needs this figure to make a decision, and the data to compute it exist.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Counter cost estimate.** Restoring output needs about 1/0.886 ≈ 13% more staff, close to the 12% stated. But adding 12% to the wage bill while restoring output should raise cost per contact by about 12%, not 9%. Perhaps new hires are on lower grades; the assumption should be stated.
- **Decay is still estimated from two points.** "Not disappeared" is well supported. Whether the gain levels off or keeps falling after 24 months is unknown, which is the same objection that applied to Varga and Holm's two-point extrapolation. The Limitations acknowledge the horizon; §3 should say it too.
- **Halden follow-up.** 9 of 23 organisations didn't respond, on top of the original attrition. The authors' "survivors twice over" framing is honest. Since Okafor co-authors this report, it would also be a natural place to correct the original working paper's description of the 70 → 61 withdrawals, which this report doesn't address.
- **Meeting baselines.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only at month six; this report gives baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2 hours). Say where they came from, for example historical calendars retrieved later.
- **No intervals** are given for resignations, appeal overturns, or the two-office meeting-audit comparison.

## What the report gets right

- **It rebuts the meta-analysis's "no decay" claim decisively.** The four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, so they can't speak to decay. The one controlled long-run study shows a decline.
- **It answers Varga and Holm on their own terms.** It meets their recommended standards (record-based output, actual hours, randomised comparison, more than 18 months) and still finds a gain with an interval clearly above zero. It also credits what they got right.
- **The meeting audit is handled well.** It is called two uncontrolled offices that suggest without establishing, and the report says outright that the trial can't distinguish reorganisation alone from reorganisation prompted by the hours cut.
- **Hours are measured both ways,** and the stricter measure is reported as the headline.

## Where the six documents now leave things

- **Coverage-bound work:** settled for practical purposes. Output falls about 10%, waits rise, and both Varden's county and Halden's retail organisations reversed course.
- **Discretionary work:** a per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists to 24 months in a randomised trial, fading somewhat, possibly less once the control contamination is accounted for. Output per employee is down roughly 3%, and cost per case is probably up. The per-hour gain is real, but it isn't free.
- **Mechanism:** fewer meetings is the leading candidate and fatigue a smaller one, with about a third unexplained. The policy-relevant question is now whether reorganising without cutting hours captures most of the gain. Only a trial with that arm can answer it.

Each document has corrected the one before it. This one mostly avoids the earlier pattern of overclaiming in the conclusion, except in its Summary ("confirms," the 12.5-to-8.5 comparison, "all coverage"). Bringing the Summary in line with the body would fix that.

Would you like the one-page synthesis of all six documents now?
